content_voiceover: This slide reviews three important facts about bypassing agents and inhibitor management logistics. The first question asks which clotting factor is absent from activated prothrombin complex concentrate, or aPCC, such as FEIBA. The correct answer is factor eight, and that absence is exactly the point, aPCC is designed for use in patients who have inhibitors against factor eight, so the product intentionally contains factors two, seven, nine, and ten instead, delivering hemostatic activity through a pathway that bypasses the need for factor eight altogether. The second question addresses the specific laboratory criteria required to declare successful immune tolerance induction and safely stop treatment. Three criteria must all be met, a persistently negative inhibitor titer below zero point six Bethesda units, factor eight recovery greater than sixty six percent of expected, not less than, and a factor eight half life of at least six hours. Getting the recovery threshold backwards is a common trap in these questions. The third question tests knowledge of the bioengineering strategies used to extend the half life of recombinant factor eight and factor nine products. All four listed modifications are legitimate approaches used in currently available extended half life products, fusion with the Fc portion of immunoglobulin, PEGylation, single chain factor eight engineered to bind von Willebrand factor, and albumin fusion.
keypoints: aPCC (FEIBA) contains factors II, VII, IX, and X, but not factor VIII
Successful ITI requires inhibitor titer under 0.6 BU, FVIII recovery over 66%, and half-life at least 6 hours
Extended half-life technologies: Fc fusion, PEGylation, VWF-binding single-chain FVIII, and albumin fusion
keypoint_voiceover: Three facts to nail down. aPCC works precisely because it lacks factor eight, containing only factors two, seven, nine, and ten. Stopping immune tolerance induction requires all three criteria together, low inhibitor titer, factor eight recovery above sixty six percent, and a half-life of six hours or more. And extended half-life factor products rely on Fc fusion, PEGylation, VWF-binding engineering, or albumin fusion, all four are real, in-use strategies.
